items.title: Reckon before battle
items.rule: Before fighting, lay the war out by five matters (the Way, heaven, ground, the general, law) and compare the two sides on seven questions. Whoever comes out ahead in the reckoning before battle wins, whoever has less does not, and having none is worse still. A second passage gives the reckoning as an ordered chain: the ground gives measurement, measurement gives quantity, quantity gives number, number gives the weighing of the sides, and the weighing gives victory.
items.words:
「兵者，國之大事，死生之地，存亡之道，不可不察也。故經之以五事，校之以七計，而索其情：一曰道，二曰天，三曰地，四曰將，五曰法。」…「道者，令民與上同意，可與之死，可與之生，而不畏危也。」…「故校之以七計而索其情，曰：主孰有道？將孰有能？天地孰得？法令孰行？兵眾孰強？士卒孰練？賞罰孰明？吾以此知勝負矣。」…「夫未戰而廟算勝者，得算多也；未戰而廟算不勝者，得算少也。多算勝，少算不勝，而況於無算乎？」 — "War is a great matter of state, the ground of life and death, the way to survival or ruin; it must be examined. So lay it out by five matters, compare it by seven reckonings, and search out the true situation: the Way, heaven, ground, the general, law… The Way is what makes the people one in intent with their superior, so that they will die with him or live with him and not fear danger… Compare by the seven reckonings: Which ruler has the Way? Which general has ability? Who has heaven and ground? Whose laws and orders are carried out? Whose troops are stronger? Whose officers and men are better trained? Whose rewards and punishments are clearer? By this I know victory and defeat… One who wins the temple reckoning before battle has gained more 算; one who does not has gained fewer. More wins, fewer does not, how much less none at all?"
「兵法：一曰度，二曰量，三曰數，四曰稱，五曰勝。地生度，度生量，量生數，數生稱，稱生勝。故勝兵若以鎰稱銖，敗兵若以銖稱鎰。」 — "In the method of war: first measurement, second quantity, third number, fourth weighing, fifth victory. Ground gives rise to measurement, measurement to quantity, quantity to number, number to weighing, weighing to victory. So a winning army is like a *yi* weighed against a *zhu*, a losing army like a *zhu* against a *yi*."
items.source: 《孫子兵法》始計第一 (l.12–18); 軍形第四 (l.59).
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Make yourself unbeatable first; win, then seek battle
items.rule: First make yourself unbeatable, then wait for the enemy to become beatable. Being unbeatable is in your own hands, being beatable is in the enemy's, and you cannot make the enemy certain to be beatable; so the winning army wins first and then seeks battle. Do not rely on the enemy not coming or not attacking; rely on having the means to meet them and on having what cannot be attacked.
items.words:
「昔之善戰者，先為不可勝，以待敵之可勝。不可勝在己，可勝在敵。故善戰者，能為不可勝，不能使敵之必可勝。故曰：勝可知，而不可為。」…「古之所謂善戰者，勝於易勝者也。」…「故善戰者，立於不敗之地，而不失敵之敗也。是故勝兵先勝而後求戰，敗兵先戰而後求勝。」 — "The skilled fighters of old first made themselves unbeatable and waited for the enemy to become beatable. Being unbeatable lies with oneself; being beatable lies with the enemy. So the skilled fighter can make himself unbeatable but cannot make the enemy certain to be beatable. Hence: victory can be known but cannot be made… Those the ancients called skilled fighters won where winning was easy… The skilled fighter stands where he cannot be defeated and does not miss the enemy's defeat. So the winning army wins first and then seeks battle; the losing army fights first and then seeks victory."
「故用兵之法，無恃其不來，恃吾有以待之；無恃其不攻，恃吾有所不可攻也。」 — "Do not rely on their not coming; rely on having the means to meet them. Do not rely on their not attacking; rely on having what cannot be attacked."
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Whole over broken; strike plans first, walled cities last
items.rule: Prefer keeping things whole to breaking them, at every scale from the state to the five-man squad. Subduing the other side's army without battle is the best of the best; a hundred victories in a hundred battles is not. Rank the targets as follows: plans highest, then alliances, then armies, and attacking walled cities lowest, as the method for when there is no alternative.
items.words: 「凡用兵之法，全國為上，破國次之；全軍為上，破軍次之；全旅為上，破旅次之；全卒為上，破卒次之；全伍為上，破伍次之。是故百戰百勝，非善之善者也；不戰而屈人之兵，善之善者也。故上兵伐謀，其次伐交，其次伐兵，其下攻城。攻城之法，為不得已。修櫓轒轀，具器械，三月而後成；距闉，又三月而後已。將不勝其忿，而蟻附之，殺士三分之一，而城不拔者，此攻之災也。故善用兵者，屈人之兵而非戰也，拔人之城而非攻也，毀人之國而非久也，必以全爭於天下，故兵不頓而利可全，此謀攻之法也。」 — "In using troops, a whole state is best, a broken one next; a whole army best, a broken one next; and so for brigade, company and squad. So a hundred victories in a hundred battles is not the best of the best; to subdue the other's army without battle is the best of the best. So the highest use of troops strikes plans, the next strikes alliances, the next strikes troops, the lowest attacks walled cities. Attacking cities is the method for when there is no alternative: three months to make shields, assault carts and equipment, three more for the earthen mounds; if the general cannot master his anger and sends the men swarming up like ants, a third of them are killed and the city still stands — this is the calamity of attack. So the skilled user of troops subdues the other's army without battle, takes the other's city without attacking it, destroys the other's state without a long war; he contends for all under heaven by keeping things whole, so his troops are not blunted and the gain can be whole."
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Know whether you can fight; know the other side and yourself
items.words:
「故知勝有五：知可以戰與不可以戰者勝，識衆寡之用者勝，上下同欲者勝，以虞待不虞者勝，將能而君不御者勝。此五者，知勝之道也。故曰：知彼知己，百戰不殆；不知彼而知己，一勝一負；不知彼不知己，每戰必殆。」 — "There are five ways to know victory: one who knows when he can fight and when he cannot wins; one who knows how to use many and few wins; one whose superiors and subordinates want the same thing wins; one who, prepared, waits for the unprepared wins; one whose general is able and whose ruler does not interfere wins. These five are the way to know victory. Hence: know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you are not in danger; not knowing the other but knowing yourself, one win, one loss; knowing neither, in every battle you are in danger."
「知吾卒之可以擊，而不知敵之不可擊，勝之半也；知敵之可擊，而不知吾卒之不可以擊，勝之半也；知敵之可擊，知吾卒之可以擊，而不知地形之不可以戰，勝之半也。…故曰：知彼知己，勝乃不殆；知天知地，勝乃可全。」 — "Knowing our troops can attack but not that the enemy cannot be attacked is half a victory; knowing the enemy can be attacked but not that our troops cannot attack is half a victory; knowing the enemy can be attacked and our troops can attack, but not that the ground does not permit battle, is half a victory… Hence: know the other and yourself, and victory is not in danger; know heaven and ground, and victory can be whole."
items.label: `quoted`

items.title: Move only when it accords with advantage; never from anger
items.rule: Do not move without advantage, do not use troops without gain, do not fight unless in danger; a ruler must not raise an army out of anger, nor a general give battle out of resentment. Move when it accords with advantage and stop when it does not. Anger can turn back into joy, but a destroyed state cannot be restored and the dead cannot be brought back.
items.words:
「夫戰勝攻取，而不修其功者凶，命曰『費留』。故曰：明主慮之，良將修之，非利不動，非得不用，非危不戰。主不可以怒而興師，將不可以慍而致戰。合於利而動，不合於利而止。怒可以復喜，慍可以復悅，亡國不可以復存，死者不可以復生。故明主慎之，良將警之，此安國全軍之道也。」 — "To win battles and take objectives without 修 the achievement is ill-omened; it is called 費留. Hence the enlightened ruler considers it and the good general attends to it: do not move without advantage, do not use troops without gain, do not fight unless in danger. A ruler must not raise an army out of anger; a general must not give battle out of resentment. Move when it accords with advantage; stop when it does not. Anger can become joy again, resentment can become pleasure again; a destroyed state cannot exist again, the dead cannot live again. So the enlightened ruler is careful of it and the good general is wary of it: this is the way to keep the state secure and the army whole." On 修 and 費留, the commentators split; see Changes #8.
The same gate is in 九地: 「合於利而動，不合於利而止。」
The bamboo 〈見吳王〉 gives the same stance in dialogue. It is in English only here; I did not open a Chinese transcription. Ames translates: "Using the military is to gain the advantage; it is not a matter of being fond of it… it is not a matter of sport."
items.source: 火攻第十二 (l.159); 九地第十一 (l.140). For 〈見吳王〉: Roger T. Ames, *Sun-tzu: The Art of Warfare* (Ballantine, 1993), Part II ch.5, from the 1985 銀雀山 edition.
items.label: `quoted` (火攻, 九地). The 〈見吳王〉 line is `attributed`: it is a narrated dialogue, and Ames judges that both it and the 史記 drill story are later than the core text.
